findings.location: Scene 1, B2, L239, against Scene 3, B9, L731
findings.passage: L239: "Terenas's boy, with an army and orcs to chase. If he had an opinion about grain at all, it would be somewhere below the orcs, and below his horse." / L731: "they'll put the flour after the orcs, and after the horses, and after the quartermaster's supper."
findings.problem: B9's new information is that Sylvanas expects the army to rank the grain below the orcs. That expectation is already on the page in B2, with the same ladder (orcs, then horse). The closing assessment therefore repeats a joke the reader has heard, and the chapter's last spoken judgment loses its edge. This is the chapter's only remaining case of a beat being pre-empted.
findings.fix: At L239, keep 'Terenas's boy, with an army and orcs to chase' and cut the ranking sentence. Replace it with something she files without judging, for example a ranger's note on the inn men's complaint (no remounts, no oats: an army that has stripped the road of horses is a big one), so that the first time she ranks the grain below the orcs is aloud to Jaina at L731. Leave L731 as it is.

findings.passage: "Anyone. Brask, Corley, the miller, the ostler at Wick, the woman sweeping the chapel step."
findings.problem: The depot was swept the night before they arrived. The woman on the chapel step was only seen after the overseer interview, on the ride north, so she could not have warned the depot. Brask is the ally they left behind them in the village. Sylvanas tracks for a living, and she would not list a witness who came after the event. As written, the 'anyone' list reads as careless rather than tired.
findings.fix: Swap the chapel-step woman for the Plough's ostler, who came out at night and 'held it up to the horses, then to their faces' (L297). He saw them hours before the depot and is already planted. You can also drop Brask or keep him; 'Anyone' still carries the hyperbole either way.

findings.passage: "She looked across at Cyndia, who was checking a girth and did not look back, seeming satisfied."
findings.problem: Dangling modifier. Grammatically, 'seeming satisfied' attaches to Cyndia, but the tell belongs to Lyriel (she checks whether her joke landed, it never does, and she is satisfied anyway). The voice-sheet beat is blurred onto the wrong ranger.
findings.fix: Make Lyriel the subject of the satisfaction, e.g. '...who was checking a girth and did not look back. Lyriel seemed satisfied with that.' Or end the sentence at 'did not look back' and let Lyriel's next action show it.

findings.passage: "It was slow. Sylvanas did not offer to take it. She would not have wanted it taken, in that state, and she would have hated whoever did it."
findings.problem: The 'she' in the last sentence is ambiguous. If it is the mage, the narration is reporting the mage's wants and hates as fact, which is mind-reading. If it is Sylvanas putting herself in that state, the line is fine, but it does not say so.
findings.fix: Anchor it to Sylvanas's own frame: 'She would not have wanted it taken, in that state. She would have hated whoever did it.' preceded by an explicit 'Herself,' or 'In the mage's place,'. Or simply: 'Sylvanas would have hated whoever took it from her.'

findings.passage: e.g. L537: "And who told him? The lord? Or whoever had the use of the lord's granaries... she'd have sent him back out to get it."
findings.problem: The style guide caps paragraphs at 100 words or 7 sentences. Most of these are only 5-19 words over, and several are tactical-analysis paragraphs, which the guide allows to run long (L419 rut read, L397 the wagon sum, L717 the road choice). The ones that would gain from a break are the interior-argument blocks (L537, L637, L525), where a break before the turning question would also sharpen it.
findings.fix: Optional. Break L537 before 'If one of her rangers had come to her with this'. Break L637 before 'She had been waiting'. Break L525 before 'She could see it.' Leave the tactical-read paragraphs long.

checksSummary.emotional-life: Pass. Sylvanas argues with herself in her own idiom in every scene. S1: 'Bad luck, then... —yes, and a free carter buys back his own spoiled flour... No. A day, every time.' (L271-273), and 'Was that trust? ... She'd take that, and call it what she liked.' (L219). S2: 'Frightened of what? ... What, then?' (L393-395), the self-flaying over 'the clock was running' (L441), and the Barov argument (L527-541), which holds the connection-not-guilt line with a ranger's yardstick. S3: the carter argument settles and then unsettles itself ('That settled it. / It didn't settle anything.' L685-687) and ends in an action. Registers: dry humour (Lyriel's loop joke, 'I can't hear paper', the fifth-legged horse, the marrow, the burnt end), exhaustion (knees, the mare going down), cold dread (the wood at L279), and grim satisfaction (the map). Every value shift lands on a concrete object or line: the wasp and the 'Nine since', 'We don't stop at the Plough', the slumped ruts, ANDORHAL laid at the narrow end of the fan, 'Jaina had been on her feet before the question was cold', the knife in the bench.
checksSummary.voice-register: Pass. The voices are distinct. Cyndia reports in the order things happened and puts her one view last, labelled ('I'd say that was on purpose', 'I'd say they were army wagons'). Lyriel opens people up with 'friend' and kettles and jokes in her observation-plus-comparison shape. Jaina is quick and exact and corrects herself without pride ('Make it heavy'). The overseer's smoothness is its own tell. Corley is clerkish and defensive. Sylvanas aloud stays clipped and finished, and inside she argues.
checksSummary.limited-third: Pass, except for the ambiguous pronoun at L119. Contamination always arrives through Jaina's staff and words. The cold Sylvanas feels is the frost cost, not the sickness.
checksSummary.dialogue-register: Pass. No institutional or clinical speech. Dialogue is about 17% of the words, below the style guide's procedural target, but the plan sets this chapter's register as paper, records and road, so this is advisory only.
checksSummary.beat-plan-fidelity: Pass. All ten beats (B1-B6a, B7-B9) are dramatized. The plan-specific requirements are met: one office and one argument over one ledger (B1); Jaina's no-pride correction at Hollow Green (B2), with a second at Ashford (B7); Lyriel's clerk joke, Jaina's laugh and Cyndia not laughing (B3); plain-sight clues left without comment (B5, with Corley's kettle as the innocent cover); the rut read anchored to the pre-dawn rain (B6); the overseer alive and gone; Barov placed by Jaina without arguing guilt; 'the mage' to 'Jaina' first at L641, with 'Proudmoore'/'Mage' kept aloud; the carter handled with correct Ch3 handles and kept apart from both the young man with the cart and Lyriel's answer; and the road chosen on Jaina's read with the re-read declined ('No.'). The only beat-level issue is the B2 pre-emption of B9's prediction.

summary: The revision fixes every fail-driver from r0: texture is at 100, the 'braced for the lecture' beat now runs setup, reinforcement and payoff only, the B9 road logic is coherent, and the Strahnbrad sources converge on the south road. Every scene keeps strong free indirect argument in Sylvanas's idiom, the voices are distinct, and all ten beats are dramatized with concrete value-shift moments. What remains is polish: the B2 thought pre-empts B9's 'grain below the orcs' prediction (medium, one-sentence fix), a leak-suspect list that names a witness seen after the leak, a dangling modifier that moves Lyriel's tell onto Cyndia, an ambiguous pronoun at L119, and a handful of slightly long paragraphs.
